Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i'm looking for a practical school-lunch plan for a fictional district, Alder Creek Public Schools, not a general essay about food. Right now around 62 percent of students take a school lunch on an average day. At the elementary schools participation is closer to 70 percent, at the middle school it's about 58 percent, and at the high school it's roughly 45 percent. We don't know whether those differences are mostly about menu preference, the lunch schedule, students bringing food from home, or something else. Don't present a cause as fact. Our current lunch prices and eligibility arrangements should be treated as unchanged; I am not asking for a price change or a new eligibility policy. The practical question is how to make meals work better within the setup we have, and what information we might need before deciding anything bigger.

The kitchens are quite different from one another. Both elementary cafeterias have ovens, refrigerators, and enough room for basic food preparation. The middle school has a small kitchen and can reheat food but has limited space for preparation. The high school has the most equipment, though its service line gets backed up when several classes arrive close together. One of the kitchen leads put it this way: “we can heat it, but we can't cook it from scratch here.” Please use that as a real operational concern, not a reason to assume every school has the same equipment. Deliveries arrive at each campus on different days, and there isn't a central district kitchen.

Staffing is tight, especially when someone is absent. Each site has a cafeteria lead, but the number of other staff on duty varies by school and day. I don't have reliable labor-hour totals, so don't make up staffing numbers or promise that extra workers can be hired. We'd like recommendations that could be tested with existing staff first, and that say when a suggestion might require additional time or training. Please include food safety and allergy procedures as part of the practical discussion. We have students with documented allergies, but I don't have a current count or a list of allergens to share, so don't guess at either one or propose a menu that assumes those details.

Families have asked for more familiar foods, more fresh fruit, and clearer information about ingredients. One parent said, “my child wants to know what's actually in the sauce.” That is feedback, not a districtwide survey result. Some families have also mentioned that students need enough time to eat. Elementary lunch periods are about 25 minutes; middle school periods are 28 minutes; high school periods are 30 minutes, although the line can reduce the time students have at a table. Please consider menu communication and serving flow along with the food itself. Don't claim we can change bell schedules; that decision isn't part of this request.

We'd also like to reduce avoidable food waste without pressuring students to finish food they don't want. Staff have noticed unopened milk and whole fruit left behind, but we haven't weighed waste by item or campus. Ask for a simple way to measure a starting point before suggesting targets. If you mention share tables, leftover food, or donation, make clear that local food-safety rules and school procedures would have to be checked first. We do not have an established donation program that you can assume is already operating.

Please include a modest approach to local purchasing, but don't assume local products are always available or cheaper. The district has used apples from a nearby grower once during the fall, but there is no standing contract, and delivery timing can be uncertain. We would like to know what could fit into a menu rotation if price, quantity, and delivery all work out. Keep the plan compatible with the nutrition requirements that apply to school meals; don't invent a special standard or claim that a particular menu meets requirements without the necessary details. We don't need recipes for a full year.

Please make the requested deliverable a practical plan rather than a finished menu. It should distinguish immediate, low-disruption steps from ideas that need more information, coordination, or money. Include a short proposed first phase of about six to eight weeks, but don't imply that the district has approved a pilot or set a start date. In one numbered section, lay out a small set of measures we could track, such as participation by school level, student feedback, wait time, and food waste; explain briefly what each would tell us. We don't currently collect all of those measures consistently, so say where a baseline would be needed. Include who might gather the information by role, not invented staff names.

Please also suggest a manageable way to hear from students and families across all four schools. We have a family council that meets monthly, but attendance is uneven, and students don't all use the same way to give feedback. Don't describe the council as representing every family. A middle school student told a cafeteria lead, “the good stuff runs out before my lunch.” That's one student's comment, not proof that stock-outs are routine. The plan can show how to check whether stock availability is an issue before recommending a fix.

End by noting the main decisions that would still need local confirmation, including available budget, current allergy procedures, campus-specific equipment and staffing, food-safety rules for any waste-reduction idea, and whether local suppliers can meet quantity and timing needs. Write for the superintendent, cafeteria leads, and family council. Address all four schools while distinguishing elementary, middle, and high school needs. ### District context
Alder Creek has two elementary schools, one middle school, and one high school, serving about 1,680 students altogether. Enrollment fluctuates during the year, so treat this as a working snapshot rather than an exact daily count. About 62 percent of students take a school lunch on an average day: participation is approximately 70 percent at the elementary schools, 58 percent at the middle school, and 45 percent at the high school. The reasons for these differences are not known. Do not state that menu preference, lunch schedules, food brought from home, or any other factor is the cause.

Treat current lunch prices and eligibility arrangements as unchanged. Do not propose a price change or new eligibility policy. Focus on improving meals within the existing setup and identifying information needed before larger decisions are made.

### Operating conditions and constraints
The campuses do not share a central kitchen, and deliveries arrive on different days. Both elementary cafeterias have ovens, refrigerators, and space for basic preparation. The middle school has a small kitchen with limited preparation space and can reheat food. The high school has the most equipment, but its service line backs up when several classes arrive close together. A kitchen lead said, “we can heat it, but we can't cook it from scratch here.” Treat this as an operational concern, and do not assume facilities are alike.

Staffing is tight, particularly during absences. Every site has a cafeteria lead, but the number of other staff on duty varies by school and day. Reliable labor-hour totals are unavailable. Do not invent staffing numbers or promise new hires. Favor suggestions that could first be tested with existing staff, and identify when an idea may require more time or training. Include practical consideration of food safety and allergy procedures. Students have documented allergies, but no current count or allergen list is available; do not guess at either or assume allergy details when discussing possible menus.

### Food, service, and waste
Families have asked for more familiar foods, more fresh fruit, and clearer ingredient information. One parent said, “my child wants to know what's actually in the sauce.” Present this as feedback, not as a districtwide survey result. Lunch periods are about 25 minutes in elementary schools, 28 minutes at the middle school, and 30 minutes at the high school. The service line can reduce students’ time at a table. Consider menu communication and serving flow as well as food. Do not claim that bell schedules can be changed; that decision is outside this request.

The district would like to reduce avoidable waste without pressuring students to finish unwanted food. Staff have noticed unopened milk and whole fruit left behind, but waste has not been weighed by item or campus. Propose a simple way to establish a baseline before recommending targets. If discussing share tables, leftovers, or donation, state that local food-safety rules and school procedures would need to be checked first. Do not assume a donation program already exists.

Include a modest approach to local purchasing. Do not assume local products are always available or less expensive. The district used apples from a nearby grower once during the fall, but has no standing contract, and delivery timing can be uncertain. Describe what might fit into a menu rotation only if price, quantity, and delivery work out. Keep recommendations compatible with applicable school-meal nutrition requirements. Do not invent a special standard or claim a menu meets requirements without the necessary details. Full-year recipes are not needed.

### Suggested first phase and feedback
Distinguish immediate, low-disruption steps from ideas that need more information, coordination, or money. Include a proposed first phase of about six to eight weeks, without implying that a pilot has been approved or a start date set.

Suggest a manageable way to hear from students and families at all four schools. The family council meets monthly, but attendance is uneven, and students do not all use the same feedback method. Do not describe the council as representing every family. A middle school student told a cafeteria lead, “the good stuff runs out before my lunch.” Treat that as one student’s comment, not proof that stock-outs are routine. Show how to check whether availability is a problem before recommending a fix.

### Measures to track
In one numbered section, propose a small set of measures, such as participation by school level, student feedback, wait time, and food waste. Briefly explain what each measure would show, and note where a baseline is needed because collection is not currently consistent. Identify possible information-gathering roles, not invented staff names.

End by listing decisions requiring local confirmation: available budget; current allergy procedures; equipment and staffing at each campus; food-safety rules for any waste-reduction idea; and whether local suppliers can meet quantity and timing needs. Keep the tone useful and realistic. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you turn this into a usable prompt for a comparison, not do the comparison itself. it’s for a fictional school lunch planning discussion at cedar valley public schools, which serves 1,240 students at three schools: Maple, with 510 students, Ridge, with 430, and Harbor, with 300. Compare the two lunch-service plans below using the criteria i’ve listed. The figures are planning estimates from a worksheet, not final prices or confirmed results, and some details are still unknown. Please keep that distinction clear. The question is how the plans compare on the supplied criteria, not which one should be chosen.

The first plan is called Cook-and-Serve. Each school would prepare lunch in its own kitchen, using the equipment already there. The worksheet estimates an average of 680 meals served per school day across all three schools, or about 55 percent of enrolled students. It lists an estimated food cost of $2.18 per meal and an estimated labor cost of $1.42 per meal, for a combined estimate of $3.60. Those figures leave out equipment replacement, and the worksheet doesn’t say whether they include the cost of kitchen utilities. The current kitchen teams total eight full-time-equivalent positions across the district. The proposal says the menus could use produce from nearby farms when available, but there isn’t a guaranteed quantity or price for that produce.

The second is called Central Prep and Delivery. Maple’s kitchen would prepare food for all three schools, and meals would go to Ridge and Harbor in insulated carriers. Its worksheet estimate is $2.04 per meal for food and $1.18 for labor, totaling $3.22, based on 720 meals served per day, about 58 percent of enrollment. It assumes two delivery vans and lists an additional $18,000 a year for fuel and maintenance, but it isn’t clear whether that annual amount is already included in the per-meal labor estimate. Ridge has a serving line but no full production kitchen, and Harbor has a small warming area. The plan notes that delivery times would need to fit each school’s lunch schedule; no delivery route or final schedule is in the materials. It also says locally purchased produce could be used, but doesn’t state how often.

Please use these comparison criteria: estimated cost per meal, student participation, nutrition and menu flexibility, food waste, staffing, and daily logistics. I want the comparison to explain what the supplied information does and doesn’t tell us under each criterion. For cost, show the food and labor estimates separately as well as the stated combined amount, and flag the $18,000 van expense question rather than deciding how it should be counted. For participation, report both daily meal estimates and the percentages of enrollment as they appear in the worksheet; don’t treat either as a guaranteed forecast. Cook-and-Serve has a note that each kitchen could adjust production during service, while Central Prep and Delivery has a note that batch sizes would be set before the vans leave. Please explain those as operational differences, not as proof that one plan wastes more or less. There is no student feedback survey attached. The staffing information for Cook-and-Serve is the district total of eight full-time-equivalent kitchen positions; the other plan’s labor estimate is given, but it doesn’t include a staff count or say whether existing positions would change. For logistics, mention that Cook-and-Serve uses three existing kitchens, while Central Prep and Delivery depends on Maple’s kitchen, two vans, insulated carriers, and serving or warming facilities at Ridge and Harbor. No information is supplied on carrier capacity, travel times, vehicle availability, or what happens if a van is late. Don’t fill those gaps in. One cafeteria manager is quoted in the notes as saying, “If the truck is late, the lunch bell still rings.” A Maple cook says, “We can use the greens when the farm has them, but I can’t promise the same amount every week.” Treat those as ordinary comments illustrating concerns, not as measurements or official findings.

There’s also a short note from the planning meeting: “The per-meal numbers are useful for a first look, but we still need to check what is inside them.” Please include that uncertainty in the prompt so the comparison doesn’t present estimates as audited totals. The source material does not say whether the plans have the same menu cycle, portion sizes, student eligibility mix, or accounting method. Those are unknown, so don’t assume they are equal or try to calculate adjusted figures. Keep the comparison focused on the six listed criteria and the information in this request. Don’t add outside benchmarks, make up missing data, assign a score, or make a recommendation.

Could the finished prompt have a short opening that states the comparison question and a numbered section with the six criteria, followed by a brief closing note about the limits of the available information? - **Central Prep and Delivery:** Maple’s kitchen would prepare food for all three schools, with meals delivered to Ridge and Harbor in insulated carriers. The worksheet estimates 720 meals per day, or about 58 percent of enrollment. Estimated food cost is $2.04 per meal and labor cost is $1.18, for a stated combined estimate of $3.22.
